# `liber:display-device@1`

Generated reference for the `liber:display-device` package (`display-device.lsidl`). See [the LSIDL language](../../../LSIDL.md).

LiberSystem display-device package - the one wire between DisplayService and a display driver.  WHY IT IS TYPED. This boundary was seven byte strings: `FB`, `FBNEW`, `RESIZE`, `FLUSH`, `PRESENT`, `OK` and `ERR`, with the framebuffer description memcpy'd out of a message at an offset and four little-endian `u32`s decoded by hand on the other side. Every other service boundary in this tree is LSIDL with typed capabilities, and this one is the boundary that hands over a MAPPED DMA BACKING - the one where a length read at the wrong offset is a mapping of the wrong size.  AND WHY ITS LIFECYCLE IS WRITTEN DOWN HERE RATHER THAN DISCOVERED. Eight questions decide whether two implementations of this wire agree, and none of them was answered anywhere:  WHO OWNS THE BACKING AND FOR HOW LONG. The DRIVER owns it. It creates the DMA object, keeps its own reference, and hands DisplayService a duplicate that is valid until the backing is REPLACED or the connection is lost. DisplayService unmaps and closes its handle on either, and a handle outliving its generation is a mapping of memory the driver may have given back.  HOW A BACKING BINDS TO A GENERATION. Every `scanout` carries a generation, and the generation changes whenever the BACKING changes - a resize that reallocates, a driver restart, a mode set. A present names the generation it was drawn for.  WHAT A RESIZE DOES. A resize that fits inside the existing backing changes the VISIBLE extent and nothing else, and the generation does not move: the same pixels are still there. A resize that needs more than the backing holds delivers a NEW backing with a NEW generation, and the old one is released by the service as soon as it has mapped the new one.  WHAT PRESENT COMPLETION MEANS. It means the DRIVER ACKNOWLEDGED THE COMMAND - the transfer and the flush were issued and answered by the device. It does NOT mean a scanout was observed: this backend has no vblank, no page-flip timing and no evidence of physical presentation, and reporting a command acknowledgement as a presentation timestamp would be reporting a fact nobody has.  WHAT DRIVER DEATH DOES TO IN-FLIGHT PRESENTS. The call fails. A present is synchronous on this wire, so there is exactly one in flight per connection and its failure is the service's answer; there is no queue to drain and no completion to deliver late.  HOW DISPLAYSERVICE FINDS A NEW BACKING AFTER A DRIVER RESTART. Through the provider catalogue, which is where it found the first one: it opens the replacement publication and calls `scanout` on it. This interface has no reconnect of its own, because a connection to a dead driver cannot carry one.  THAT THE EVENT STREAM IS BOUNDED. `events` is a bounded channel like every other stream in this tree. A driver that produces events faster than the service consumes them loses the OLDEST, and that is safe for exactly these events: a resize and a replacement are both idempotent snapshots of the current state, so the newest one is the true one.  AND THAT A BACKING FROM AN OLD GENERATION CAN NEVER BE PRESENTED INTO A NEW ONE. A present naming a generation that is not the current one is refused with `stale`, not clamped, not drawn, and not silently accepted - it is a frame drawn against pixels that no longer exist.

## Types

### record `scanout`

The scanout backing a driver hands over: where the pixels are, what they are, how much of them is visible, and which generation they belong to.

| field | type | description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `backing` | `buffer` | The DMA backing, as a handle the service maps. The driver keeps its own reference; this one is valid until the backing is replaced or the connection is lost. |
| `layout` | `image-layout` | What the backing's pixels are. The extent here is the ALLOCATED one, which a driver may make larger than the display so a later resize needs no new backing. |
| `visible` | `extent-2d` | How much of the backing the display actually shows. Never larger than the layout's extent. |
| `generation` | `u32` | Which generation these pixels belong to. It changes whenever the BACKING changes. |

### variant `device-event`

What a driver reports between calls.

| tag | case | payload | description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | `resized` | `extent-2d` | The display size changed INSIDE the existing backing. The generation has not moved and the pixels are the same pixels. |
| 1 | `replaced` | `scanout` | The backing was replaced: a new object, a new generation, and the old handle is the service's to release once it has mapped this one. |

## Interfaces

### interface `display-device`

The display device, as DisplayService drives it.

Request `[op u16][corr u32][args]`, reply `[corr u32][result]`.

| op | method | signature | description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | `scanout` | `scanout() -> result<scanout, error>` | The current scanout. Called once at adoption and again after a rebind; a driver that cannot supply one answers `unavailable` rather than an empty backing. |
| 2 | `present` | `present(generation: u32, damage: damage-region) -> result<unit, error>` | Transfer the damaged pixels and flush them to the device, answering when the device has acknowledged BOTH. `generation` is the generation the frame was drawn for: a present naming a generation that is no longer current is refused rather than drawn. |
| 3 | `events` | `events() -> stream<device-event>` | The bounded event stream: resizes and replacements. |
